questions.question: What is the general form of a power series centred at $a$?
questions.explanation: A power series centred at $a$ has the general form $\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} c_n(x-a)^n$.
questions.source_support: The definition gives the form $\sum_{n = 0}^{\infty} c_n(x-a)^n$.

$\sum c_n(x+a)$ has no power $n$ on $(x+a)$.

They must eventually become equal to $a$

questions.question: Why does the formal expression $\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} c_n(x-a)^n$ not by itself tell you where the power series converges?
options: Every expression of this form converges for all real $x$.
The definition gives the form of the series; convergence depends on the coefficients and the value of $x$.
Every expression of this form diverges unless all coefficients are zero, in all instances without exception.
A power series is only defined after its exact sum is known.
